content: The use of multiple lumen umbilical venous catheters (ML-UVCs) instead of single lumen umbilical venous catheters (SL-UVCs) in newborns may reduce the need for additional venous access lines. However, the associated complication rates between these two types of catheters may differ. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of ML-UVCs compared to SL-UVCs in newborn infants. Specifically, the study aimed to assess the need for additional vascular access, the rates of complications, and the impact on morbidity and mortality. To gather evidence, randomized and quasi-randomized trials were identified through searches of multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Science Direct, covering publications up to February 2005. Additionally, abstracts from scientific meetings published in Pediatric Research (1990-2004) were manually reviewed, and subject experts were contacted to identify unpublished or ongoing studies. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing the safety and efficacy of ML-UVCs versus SL-UVCs in neonates (both term and preterm) requiring umbilical venous catheter insertion within the first four weeks of life. Data extraction was performed independently by each review author, and any discrepancies were resolved through discussion. The outcomes assessed included the total number of additional peripheral intravenous lines (PIVs) required per infant during the first week and the first four weeks of life, the number of additional central venous lines (placed percutaneously or surgically) required per infant during the first four weeks, and other safety and efficacy measures. Risk ratios (RR), risk differences (RD), and weighted mean differences (WMD) were calculated with 95% confidence intervals (CI). If RD was statistically significant, the number needed to treat (NNT) or number needed to harm (NNH) was also calculated. Three studies met the inclusion criteria for this review (Khilnani 1991; Loisel 1996; Soupre 1998). The results showed that the use of ML-UVCs was associated with a reduction in the number of additional PIVs required during the first week of life [WMD -1.42, 95% CI -1.74 to -1.10, p < 0.00001, n = 99]. However, there was no significant difference in the number of additional PIVs required during the first four weeks of life [MD -2.30, 95% CI -6.65 to 2.05, n = 36]. The ML-UVC group experienced an increase in catheter malfunctions compared to the SL-UVC group [typical RR 3.69, 95% CI 0.99 to 13.81, p = 0.05; RD 0.15, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.27, p = 0.01; NNH = 7, 95% CI 4 to 33, n = 99]. Other outcomes, including clinical sepsis, catheter-related bloodstream infections, catheter-associated thrombosis, complications related to catheter malposition in the heart and great vessels, necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), and early neonatal mortality, did not show significant differences between the two groups. The authors concluded that while ML-UVCs reduce the need for PIVs during the first week of life, they are associated with an increased risk of catheter malfunctions. Due to the poor quality of the included randomized studies and the imprecision in estimating clinically significant complications, no definitive recommendations can be made regarding the choice between ML-UVCs and SL-UVCs. Further well-designed, adequately powered, randomized, and blinded controlled trials are necessary to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of ML-UVCs (including double and triple lumen catheters) compared to SL-UVCs. These future studies should also consider the impact of the type of catheter material used.
